newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Treasuries end lower, 10-yr sale disappoints.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Treasuries end lower, 10-yr sale disappoints.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries closed lower for the second day in a row on Tuesday as investors sold after the results of a key Treasury auction failed to meet the market's most bullish expectations, analysts said.
The 6-3/4 percent benchmark 30-year U.S. Treasury bond ended down 7/32 at 99-9/32 to yield 6.81 percent.

"We had a little rally from noon to one o'clock on excitement that the 10-year was going to see some strong demand. But the market's hopes were dashed," said Chris Rupkey, economist at Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi.
The Treasury sold $10 billion in 10-year notes on Tuesday at 6.502 percent. The sale's bid-to-cover ratio was at 2.34. Non-competitive bids totalled $284 million.
"The results were kind of on the soft side," Rupkey said.
Analysts said the short-lived rally before the auction's bidding deadline at 1300 EDT/1700 GMT was triggered by rumors that a large foreign player was bidding heavily at the tender.
"We had some very interesting price behaviour around the bidding deadline...most of it was a rumored big buyer in the auction. A buyer out of Japan, actually," an analyst said.
"But the rumored buying was not evident when the auction result came out. That's why the market backed up," said the analyst, who works at a foreign investment bank here.
The market shrugged off the mostly friendly economic indicators released on Tuesday, which included the Richmond Federal Reserve survey and retail sales gauges.
"The numbers were mostly a non-event today," said Patrick Dimick, economist at C.S. First Boston.
The Richmond Fed manufacturing shipments index fell to 2 in September from 16 in August. The service revenues index fell in September to minus two from 21 in August.

U.S. chain store sales fell 0.1 percent in the seven-day period ended October 5 as measured by the BTM/Schroders weekly index. The Redbook retail sales index fell 0.4 percent in the five weeks of fiscal September.
Analysts said the market is likely to remain rangebound on Wednesday ahead of the release of two key economic indicators on Friday: the September producer price index (PPI) and retail sales.
In a recent Reuters survey, U.S. economists said they expect overall PPI to rise 0.3 percent, while the core rate -- which excludes food and energy -- is seen up 0.2 percent.
September retail sales are expected to rise 0.2 percent. The ex-autos number is seen up 0.3 percent.

Analysts said the benchmark bond yield is expected to trade within a range of 6.73 and 6.82 percent. The yield curve flattened somewhat on Tuesday with the spread between the two-year notes and the bellwether narrowing to 88 basis points from 89 points on Monday.
The three-month Treasury bill rate closed up one basis point at 5.00 percent. The six-month bill rate rose one point to 5.10 percent. The year bill rate was up two points at 5.25 percent.

The two-year note closed down 2/32 at 100-4/32, yielding 5.93 percent. The five-year note traded off 4/32 at 100-12/32 to yield 6.29 percent. The ten-year note closed down 5/32 at 103-7/32, yielding 6.55 percent.
